text:
Rain (1932)
***1/2
This is a simple story of good vs evil. It pits a jazzy prostitute against an evangelist reformer.
If you’re expecting an old movie like this to be safe viewing for Nana and her church crowd, you’d better buckle up.
Joan Crawford stars as Sadie Thompson: a hard-drinking sassy chick. She is on an ocean liner headed to the South Pacific, looking to get as far away from uptight civilization as possible.
On the same ship, unfortunately, is Alfred Davidson (Walter Huston). He is a missionary who is trying to bring uptight civilization to the far corners of the world.
Due to a cholera outbreak, the ship is forced to stop on the rainy island of Pago Pago.
The town has one little inn. So sexy Sadie and domineering Davidson are going to be housemates for a while. And as the great poet Daffy Duck used to say: This means war.
The neighborly conflict starts slowly. Sadie does her thing, playing music and drinking and carousing in her room. Davidson and his pearl-clutching wife stew in anger about having to listen to all the fun.
“Mrs. Davidson tells me that she hasn’t closed her eyes ever since that girl came to live under the same roof as her,” a guest observes to her husband. “The founder of her religion wasn’t so squeamish,” he retorts.
Director Lewis Milestone (“All Quiet on the Western Front”) certainly prefers carefree fun to righteous judgment. But that isn’t the point of “Rain.” This is not an anti-Christian movie. It is an anti-Christian-activism movie.
Way back when, Christianity viewed passively dying at the hands of the government as the apex of morality (Jesus, Paul, Peter, Stephen, Sebastian).
In the Progressive Era, the film laments, Christianity had come full circle. Some Christians were using the full power of earthly government to oppress pagans and sinners.
It was bad enough that Temperance do-gooders had meddled with America. “We live in the day of the new Commandment,” one guy chuckles. “Thou shalt not enjoy thyself.”
But now self-righteous reformers were crisscrossing the globe, stamping out religious diversity and freedom. We don’t loathe Alfred Davidson for asking Sadie to turn off her loud music on the Sabbath. We loathe him because he goes to the governor of Pago Pago to strongarm the powerless prostitute.
I’ve heard of the threat of “Christian Nationalism” in the 21st Century, but I have no fear. To my eyes, materialist secularism has fully triumphed. 2026 America is nothing like a prudish theocracy. We are society of casinos and weed stores and dance clubs and unlimited premarital sex with anyone you want.
“Rain” takes us back to a time when self-righteous bible thumpers were a clear and present threat to liberty.
For director Lewis Milestone, this wasn’t a political opinion: it was very personal. Just two years later, the Hays Code severely restricted the topics and themes that American filmmakers were allowed to address in their movies. The shocking climax of “Rain,” where Davidson rapes Sadie, would be completely unacceptable in 1935.
